gradepilot.title: From a GPA Calculator to GradePilot
gradepilot.subtitle: How a small academic problem became a full-stack learning project.

sections.heading: Where It Started
paragraphs: GradePilot started with a problem I could relate to: calculating university results was not always straightforward. I wanted a simpler way to work through GPA and CGPA calculations without repeating the same manual steps.

The earliest idea was modest—a calculator that could take course information and produce useful academic results. But as I worked on it, I began thinking about what students might need beyond a single calculation.

sections.heading: Growing Beyond the Calculator
paragraphs: I gradually expanded GradePilot into a more complete application. Instead of calculating a result and immediately losing it, I wanted users to be able to return to their information and understand their academic progress.

That direction introduced new responsibilities: authentication, persistent data, result organization, and clearer interfaces. The project became an opportunity to connect frontend work with backend development.

sections.heading: The Authentication Challenge
paragraphs: One of the most memorable difficulties was integrating Better Auth. Getting the authentication flow working across the application took several hours of debugging.

It pushed me to pay more attention to how sessions, requests, configuration, and frontend behavior interact. The experience also reminded me that integrating a library is not always as simple as following a short example.

sections.heading: Understanding the Calculation Logic
paragraphs: Academic calculations require more than an attractive form. Grading rules and edge cases matter, and an incorrect result can make the entire feature unreliable.

I used documentation, examples, and AI-assisted suggestions while exploring the implementation, but I also spent time understanding the grading rules and reviewing the calculation approach rather than treating generated logic as automatically correct.

sections.heading: What I Learned
paragraphs: GradePilot strengthened my understanding of how a project grows from a focused feature into a connected application. It gave me more practical experience with authentication, data persistence, and user-focused interface decisions.
It also taught me to take debugging seriously. A feature can look simple from the outside while requiring substantial investigation behind the scenes.

sections.heading: Where I Want to Take It
paragraphs: I would like to explore academic schedules, routines, and additional student-focused tools in the future.
For now, GradePilot represents an important part of my development journey: starting with a real problem, expanding the idea, and learning through the difficulties that followed.

zapshift.title: Learning Full-Stack Workflows with ZapShift
zapshift.subtitle: Exploring authentication, data, and logistics-focused interfaces.

sections.heading: The Project Idea
paragraphs: ZapShift was built as part of my full-stack web development learning journey. Parcel delivery systems are interesting because they connect multiple workflows: users, parcels, locations, and administrative operations.
I approached the project as an opportunity to understand how these connected pieces could work together inside a web application.

sections.heading: Connecting the Pieces
paragraphs: The project involved React on the frontend, backend APIs, MongoDB for application data, and Firebase for authentication.
Working across these layers helped me understand how frontend interfaces depend on backend responses and how application state changes as users perform different actions.

sections.heading: Thinking About Roles and Locations
paragraphs: Delivery-oriented applications often need different interfaces for different responsibilities. Exploring role-oriented workflows made me think more carefully about how information and actions should be organized.
I also worked with map-related interfaces using React Leaflet. This introduced a different type of UI problem compared with traditional forms and content layouts.

sections.heading: Challenges Along the Way
paragraphs: Connecting frontend functionality with backend APIs and database operations required careful debugging. Problems were not always isolated to a single component, so I had to think about how requests, responses, authentication, and stored data interacted.
The project reinforced the importance of building and verifying one workflow at a time.

sections.heading: Lessons and Future Direction
paragraphs: ZapShift helped me gain experience with larger application structures and the coordination required between frontend and backend code.
I would like to continue refining delivery-related workflows, validation, and tracking functionality while improving overall usability.

noxcodec.title: Building NoxCodec: Morse Code Meets the Terminal
noxcodec.subtitle: A small curiosity turned into an interactive frontend experiment.

sections.heading: A Curiosity About Morse Code
paragraphs: NoxCodec began with my curiosity about Morse code. The idea of representing communication through dots, dashes, and sound felt both technical and creative.
I wanted to build something that let people experiment with Morse code without needing a complicated interface.

sections.heading: Choosing the Visual Direction
paragraphs: I chose a terminal-inspired interface because it fit the project's theme. Rather than creating a plain text converter, I wanted the experience to feel like a small communication tool.
At the same time, I tried to keep the core interactions understandable: enter text, see the conversion, and explore the audio output.

sections.heading: Working with Conversion and Sound
paragraphs: Morse encoding and decoding involve different input patterns. Supporting both directions meant thinking about how text and signals should be interpreted and displayed.
Audio playback added another layer of interaction. The timing of dots, dashes, and pauses matters because Morse code is not just a visual format.

sections.heading: What Made It Interesting
paragraphs: Unlike my larger full-stack projects, NoxCodec focuses on frontend behavior and presentation. That made it a useful exercise in building responsive interactions without relying on a backend.
It also gave me an opportunity to combine a technical topic with a more distinctive visual identity.

sections.heading: Ideas for the Future
paragraphs: One idea I would like to explore is a messaging experience where Morse code becomes part of the communication process.
I also want to improve playback controls and accessibility so the project remains useful beyond its visual theme.

tuition-finder.title: Tuition Finder and the Importance of Clear Requirements
tuition-finder.subtitle: An unfinished project that taught me lessons beyond code.

sections.heading: How It Began
paragraphs: Tuition Finder began after a local client approached me about a tuition-related website. The initial idea appeared relatively simple and focused on frontend information.
As conversations continued, the expected scope expanded toward a full-stack application.

sections.heading: When the Scope Changed
paragraphs: Moving from a frontend concept with static data to a more complete application changed the amount of work and planning required.
The project involved exploring React, Firebase authentication, backend APIs, and MongoDB. However, the requirements were not consistently finalized.

sections.heading: The Difficult Part Was Not Only Technical
paragraphs: The biggest lesson was about communication and scope. It is difficult to estimate or complete work when the expected features continue changing without a clearly agreed plan.
Eventually, communication with the prospective client stopped. The project was not completed, accepted, or delivered as paid client work.

sections.heading: What I Took Away
paragraphs: The experience helped me understand why requirements, deliverables, timelines, and expectations should be clarified before development goes too far.
It also reminded me that unfinished projects can still provide useful learning, as long as their status is represented accurately.

sections.heading: What Comes Next
paragraphs: Tuition Finder remains an incomplete project. If I return to it, I would first define a smaller, verifiable set of features and complete those before expanding the application.
My priority would be finishing the main discovery workflows, validation, and a reliable user experience.
